sources.entry: ioBroker - Integration platform for the Internet of Things, focused on building automation, smart metering, ambient assisted living, process automation, visualization and data logging. (Source Code) MIT Nodejs
ioBroker | Integration platform for the Internet of Things

summary.one_liner: ioBroker is an integration platform for the Internet of Things, aimed at building automation, smart metering, ambient assisted living, process automation, visualization and data logging.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes ioBroker as a concept and database schema rather than a single application, with a common set of rules for pairs of databases that exchange data and publish events between systems. It keeps objects (metadata and configuration) and states (values) in an in-memory database that is saved to disk at intervals, or in Redis, which also serves as a publish/subscribe message broker. Systems connect through adapters, which are separate processes that can run on any host reachable over IP and can be written in nearly any language. ioBroker spawns a Node.js process per adapter instance. The README says the js-controller runs on any hardware and OS that runs Node.js, and points to the ioBroker website for the adapter list. Installation is via npx @iobroker/install on Linux or Windows.
how_to_run: Windows: mkdir C:\iobroker && cd C:\iobroker && npx @iobroker/install
See the ioBroker documentation and Command Reference for install, fix, diag and node-update parameters
notable: Adapter architecture: each connected system runs as a separate adapter process that can live anywhere on the network
Objects and states can be stored in memory or in Redis
Each adapter instance runs as its own Node.js process
Installable on Linux and Windows through an npx installer
caveats: README advises against exposing ioBroker databases, adapters or smart home devices directly to the internet; use HTTPS with valid certificates, VPN, VLAN or reverse proxy if web admin is exposed
RAM can be limiting since each adapter instance uses roughly 10 to 60 MB
Logos are copyrighted and may not be used without permission; other adapters can have different licenses
